meta.name: Briard First Year Costs
meta.excerpt: The Briard is a large, long-coated herding breed with significant grooming, food, and veterinary costs. This guide breaks down the full first-year budget for new Briard owners.
meta.meta_description: Briard first year costs: puppy price, grooming expenses, food, vet bills, and long-term ownership cost estimates for this ancient French herding breed.

intro.label: Upfront Costs
intro.heading: Getting Started with a Briard
intro.html:
• Puppy from reputable breeder: $1,500–$2,500
  • Rescue adoption fee: $200–$500
  • Large wire crate with divider: $80–$150
  • Dog bed: $60–$120
  • Stainless steel bowls: $30–$60
  • Collar, ID tag, leash: $40–$80
  • Long training line: $20–$40
  • Grooming kit (pin brush, wide comb, mat splitter, detangling spray): $90–$170
  • Baby gates / exercise pen: $50–$120
  • Toys and chews: $50–$100
  • Initial vet visit: $80–$160

Estimated Upfront Total: $2,200–$3,500

care.label: First Year Recurring
care.heading: Annual Ongoing Costs for the Briard
care.html:
• Puppy vaccination series: $200–$400
  • Spay/neuter: $300–$700
  • Parasite prevention: $200–$400/year
  • Annual wellness exam: $100–$200
  • Dog food (large breed): $900–$1,400/year
  • Treats: $150–$250/year
  • Professional grooming (5–6 visits/year): $90–$160/visit = $450–$960/year
  • Training classes: $200–$600
  • Pet insurance: $50–$85/month = $600–$1,020/year
  • Toys and enrichment: $120–$250/year
  • Boarding or pet sitting: $400–$800/year

Estimated Recurring Year-One Total: $3,620–$6,980

special.label: Total & Ongoing
special.heading: Total First Year and Long-Term Briard Costs
special.html:
Total First Year Estimate: $3,800–$6,500

After the first year, expect annual costs of $2,200–$3,800. The Briard's large size and grooming requirements keep ongoing costs higher than small or short-coated breeds.

Additional Health Cost Considerations:

  • Hip dysplasia surgery: $3,500–$7,000+ per hip if needed
  • GDV (bloat) emergency surgery: $3,000–$7,000+. Discuss prophylactic gastropexy at spay/neuter to dramatically reduce this risk.
  • Eye specialist visits (CSNB/PRA monitoring): $200–$400 per visit
  • Cancer treatment (if needed): $2,000–$15,000+ depending on type and stage
  • Professional dental cleaning: $500–$950 every 1–3 years

Grooming at Home vs. Professional: Pet owners who learn to bathe and groom their Briard at home can reduce professional grooming costs from $450–$960/year to the cost of supplies ($80–$150 annually). This requires a quality blow dryer, proper tools, and time investment — but can save $300–$800/year over the dog's lifetime.

Lifetime Cost Estimate (10–12 years): $28,000–$52,000+ depending heavily on health outcomes and grooming approach.

faq.q: What is the most expensive aspect of owning a Briard?
faq.a: For most owners, grooming is the largest ongoing expense beyond food — professional grooming at $90–$160 per visit, 5–6 times per year, adds up to $450–$960 annually. Owners who learn to groom at home can significantly reduce this cost. Potential health issues (bloat, hip dysplasia, cancer) represent the largest unpredictable costs.

faq.q: Is pet insurance worth it for a Briard?
faq.a: Yes, strongly recommended. The Briard's GDV risk alone justifies insurance — emergency bloat surgery can cost $3,000–$7,000+. The breed's cancer risk and potential for orthopedic issues further support having comprehensive coverage from puppyhood. Monthly premiums of $50–$85 represent significant financial protection.

faq.q: Can I save money by grooming my Briard at home?
faq.a: Yes — learning to groom your Briard at home represents one of the most meaningful cost savings available. With the right tools and practice, you can perform bath, blow-dry, and brush-out at home and reduce professional visits to every 3–4 months for trimming only. The initial tool investment ($150–$300) pays off within the first year.
